decisions.quote: Our results supported Gebauer et al.’s original conclusions that mind-body practices increase self-enhancement. Although the self-centrality effects were not clearly replicated in either experiment, we found evidence that measurement and sampling differences may explain this discrepancy.
decisions.location: abstract (lines 37-39); see also Statement of Relevance (lines 141-145) and General Discussion (lines 908-912, 939-941, 972-974)
decisions.reason: Gebauer et al. (2018) tested two core claims: that mind-body practices increase self-enhancement (opposing the ego-quieting hypothesis) and that they do so by increasing the self-centrality of practice-relevant behaviors (which mediates the self-enhancement effect). In the two replication experiments, the authors explicitly report that the self-enhancement findings replicated while the self-centrality effects and mediation via self-centrality 'were not clearly replicated in either experiment' (failing to replicate at a statistically significant level in the new samples as a whole, and replicating unconditionally only when pooling the original German data with the replication data in an integrative data analysis). The concluding statement in the General Discussion ('generally provides strong replication evidence for a novel, counterintuitive finding') refers to the counterintuitive self-enhancement finding and qualifies support for the self-centrality principle as resting 'particularly when all available data were analyzed together' (including the original data). Because one central tested finding replicated in the new samples and another central tested finding was explicitly marked by the authors as not clearly replicated in the replication experiments themselves, the outcome is 'mixed'.
